items.prompt: What is a class in object-oriented programming?

options.label: A blueprint defining the data and behaviour that its objects will have
A standalone function that takes inputs and returns a computed result
A single running instance that is stored in memory with its own values
A variable that holds exactly one simple value such as a number

rubric: A class is the blueprint from which objects are created.
Describing a running instance confuses the class with an object.

items.prompt: Which term names bundling data and methods together while restricting direct access to the data?

options.label: Polymorphism
Encapsulation
Inheritance
Instantiation

rubric: Encapsulation bundles state with behaviour and controls access.
Inheritance is about reusing a parent class, not hiding data.

items.prompt: What is it called when a new class reuses the fields and methods of an existing class?

options.label: Composition
Instantiation
Serialization
Inheritance

rubric: Inheritance lets a subclass acquire members of a parent class.
Instantiation creates an object; it does not reuse a class's members.

items.prompt: What is a method in OOP?

options.label: A private value that every object of a class must share
A function defined in a class that works on that class's objects
A comment block that explains what a class is meant to do and how to use it
A copy of a class that is made when a program starts running

rubric: A method is a function belonging to a class.
Confusing methods with data or documentation ignores that they are behaviour.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a constructor?

options.label: To copy all methods from a parent class into a child class so they can be reused
To convert an object into text so it can be printed out
To delete an object once the program no longer needs it
To set up a newly created object with its starting state

rubric: A constructor runs on creation to set up initial state.
Deleting is the job of destructors or garbage collection, not constructors.

items.prompt: Which of the following are commonly named core concepts of object-oriented programming? Select all that apply.

options.label: Compilation
Abstraction
Recursion
Encapsulation
Polymorphism

rubric: Encapsulation, polymorphism and abstraction (plus inheritance) are core OOP concepts.
Compilation and recursion are general programming ideas, not OOP pillars.

items.prompt: A learner reads this code: `class Car { int speed; void accelerate() { speed = speed + 10; } }`. The line `Car myCar = new Car();` is then added to the program. What is `myCar` called?

options.label: An object, an instance of the Car class
A constructor that is defined inside the Car class
A subclass that inherits from the Car class
A method that belongs to the Car class

rubric: `new Car()` creates an instance, which `myCar` refers to.
Calling it a class or method mixes up blueprint, behaviour and instance.

items.prompt: Why is it usually good practice to make a class's fields private and expose them through methods?

options.label: Private fields use less memory than public fields do at run time
Private fields let other classes inherit the data without writing code
The class can check values and keep its own state valid and consistent
Private fields stop the compiler from needing to check any types

rubric: Controlled access lets the class enforce its rules on its own data.
Memory and type checking are not what privacy is for.

items.prompt: `Circle` and `Square` both override `area()` from `Shape`. A list holds one of each, typed as `Shape`, and the program calls `area()` on every item. What happens?

options.label: Only the first item runs and the others are skipped silently
Each object runs its own class's version of `area()`
The program fails because the list mixes two different types
Both items run the `area()` version written in `Shape`

rubric: Polymorphism picks the overriding method based on the actual object.
Running the parent version ignores dynamic dispatch.

items.prompt: A `Car` object contains an `Engine` object as one of its parts. How is this relationship best classified?

options.label: Inheritance, because Car is a kind of Engine
Polymorphism, because Car and Engine can both be used through one shared interface
Encapsulation, because Engine's data is hidden inside the Car object
Composition, because a Car has an Engine as a part

rubric: Has-a relationships are composition; is-a relationships are inheritance.
Saying Car is a kind of Engine reverses the is-a test.

items.prompt: Which statement best explains abstraction?

options.label: Exposing the essential operations while hiding how they work
Bundling data with its methods so outside code cannot change that data directly
Letting a new class reuse and extend the behaviour of an existing class
Letting one method call behave differently depending on the object's type

rubric: Abstraction shows what an object does and hides how it does it.
Public fields and copied code do the opposite of hiding detail.

items.prompt: A `Counter` class has a field `count` starting at 0 and a method `increment()`. Objects `a` and `b` are created, then `a.increment()` is called twice. What is `b.count`?

options.label: Undefined, because b has not called any method yet
0, because each object has its own count field
2, because all objects of a class share one count field
1, because the two increments are divided between the objects

rubric: Instance fields belong to each object separately.
Assuming a shared field confuses instance state with class-level state.

items.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of encapsulating a class's data behind methods? Select all that apply.

options.label: Setter methods can reject invalid values before they are stored
The class's internals can change without breaking code that uses it
Classes no longer need any methods in order to be useful
Programs always run faster than ones that use public fields

rubric: Encapsulation allows validation and safe changes to internals.
Speed gains and removing methods are not benefits of encapsulation.

items.prompt: A developer defines an abstract class `Payment` with an abstract method `pay()`, plus subclasses `CardPayment` and `CashPayment` that each implement `pay()`. Writing `new Payment()` gives a compile error. Why does the error occur?

options.label: Abstract classes are incomplete, so they can't be instantiated
A parent class can only be instantiated after all of its subclasses have been instantiated first
An abstract class can only be created through a subclass reference, never through its own name
Abstract methods can only be called from inside private fields

rubric: An abstract class has unimplemented behaviour, so only concrete subclasses can be instantiated.
Creation order and reserved names are unrelated to the error.

items.prompt: What does encapsulation mainly achieve in a class?

options.label: It lets a class reuse the fields and methods of another class, so shared code is written once
It bundles data with methods and hides internals so state changes only through the class
It lets one method name behave differently for different object types, chosen when the call runs
It shows only a simplified outline of a concept and leaves out detail that users do not need

rubric: Encapsulation bundles data with methods and restricts direct access to internal state.
Reuse describes inheritance, different behaviour per type describes polymorphism, and simplified outlines describe abstraction.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between a class and an object?

options.label: A class is a blueprint, and an object is one instance built from it with its own field values
A class holds only methods and no data, while each object holds only the data that those methods use
An object is a blueprint, and a class is one copy made from it with its own separate field values
A class is a running program, and objects are the files it reads and loads when it starts up

rubric: A class defines structure and behaviour; each object is an instance with its own state.
Distractors reverse the roles or wrongly split data and methods between class and object.

items.prompt: A class is declared as `class Dog extends Animal`. What does this mean?

options.label: Animal receives all of Dog's methods, so Animal objects can bark too
Dog gets Animal's accessible fields and methods and can add or override
Dog holds an Animal object in a private field and must call its methods through that field
Dog and Animal share one set of field values across all of their instances

rubric: Inheritance gives the subclass the parent's accessible members, which it may extend or override.
Distractors reverse the direction of inheritance or confuse it with composition or shared static state.

items.prompt: A loop calls `shape.area()` on a list holding both Circle and Square objects. Why does this work?

options.label: The first object's area() is looked up once and then reused for every later object in the list
The loop copies the area() code from Circle into Square objects before it starts running
Circle and Square must be the same class for them to share a method name like area()
Each object runs its own class's version of area(), chosen by its actual type

rubric: Polymorphism lets the same call run different implementations depending on the object's type.
Distractors assume code copying, a single shared class or a one-time lookup.

items.prompt: An abstract class Vehicle declares an abstract method `move()`. What does this tell its concrete subclasses?

options.label: They must supply their own move(), so callers can rely on it existing
Vehicle objects can be created directly and given a move() later on
Vehicle.move() runs automatically whenever any subclass object is created
Subclasses may not define move() because Vehicle already owns that name

rubric: An abstract method is a promise that concrete subclasses will implement it.
Distractors treat it as an auto-run method, a ban on overriding, or something that allows direct instantiation.

items.prompt: A class keeps its fields private and exposes setters that validate input. Which are real benefits of this design? Select all that apply.

options.label: Constructors are no longer needed to initialise objects
The fields are read faster than public fields would be
Invalid values can be rejected in one place instead of everywhere
The class can no longer be subclassed by other classes
The class's internal representation can change without breaking callers

rubric: Private state behind methods centralises validation and lets internals change safely.
Speed, removing constructors and blocking subclassing are not effects of encapsulation.

items.prompt: A team's Account class has a public `balance` field. A bug report shows another class set `balance` to -500 directly. A teammate says the Account class itself has no bug in its own methods. What does this situation best show?

options.label: Public fields let outside code skip the rules; a private balance changed only via withdraw() enforces them
Objects should hold no data of their own, so balance belongs in a separate global variable that every class can read
Polymorphism would let the other class call a safer balance method automatically, even when it writes the field directly
Inheritance is needed so that a subclass can override the field and stop negative values from being set on Account

rubric: Public state lets outside code bypass invariants; encapsulation enforces them via methods.
Other distractors name OOP ideas that do not address uncontrolled direct access.

items.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

```
class Animal:
    def speak(self): return "..."
class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self): return "Meow"
print(Animal().speak() + Cat().speak())
```

options.label: MeowMeow
...Meow
Meow...

rubric: Animal().speak() gives '...' and Cat's overriding method gives 'Meow', joined in that order.
Distractors swap the order or ignore the override or the parent version.

items.prompt:
What does this Python code print?

```
class Counter:
    def __init__(self): self.n = 0
    def add(self): self.n += 1
a = Counter(); b = Counter()
a.add(); a.add(); b.add()
print(a.n, b.n)
```
rubric: Each object has its own n, so a is incremented twice and b once.
Distractors assume the field is shared between instances.

options.label: AttributeError

rubric: super().__init__() sets x to 1 first, so y is 2.
AttributeError would occur only if the parent constructor were not called.

items.prompt: You are modelling a Car that has an Engine with a `start()` method. Which structure fits this relationship?

options.label: Engine's fields become public static so Car can reach them
Car holds an Engine object in a field and calls its start()
Engine extends Car so every engine also gets wheels and doors
Car extends Engine so it inherits start() and can reuse it directly

rubric: A car has an engine, so composition with delegation fits better than inheritance.
Distractors use inheritance for a has-a relationship or break encapsulation.

items.prompt: A BankAccount keeps a private `_balance` that must never go negative. Which body of `withdraw(self, amt)` enforces this?

options.label: `self._balance -= amt`
`if amt >= 0: self._balance = amt`
`if amt > 0 and amt >= self._balance: self._balance -= amt`
`if 0 < amt <= self._balance: self._balance -= amt`

rubric: Only the last guard checks that the amount is positive and no more than the balance before subtracting.
Distractors skip the check, invert it, or overwrite the balance.

items.prompt:
Given this Python code, which statements are true for `d = Dog("Rex")`? Select all that apply.

```
class Pet:
    def __init__(self, name): self.name = name
    def describe(self): return "Pet " + self.name
class Dog(Pet):
    def describe(self): return "Dog " + self.name
```

options.label: `d.describe()` returns "Dog Rex"
`isinstance(d, Pet)` is True
`Dog()` with no argument works
`Pet("Rex").describe()` returns "Dog Rex"
`d.name` is "Rex" because Dog inherits Pet's constructor

rubric: Dog overrides describe, inherits __init__, and is an instance of Pet.
Pet's own describe returns 'Pet Rex', and the inherited constructor still requires a name.

items.prompt: A program loops over a list of notifiers and calls `n.send(msg)` on each. It already has EmailNotifier and PushNotifier classes. You now need to add an SmsNotifier that works in the same loop without changing the loop. What should you do?

options.label: Define a separate sms_send(msg) function and update the loop to call it whenever the object is an SmsNotifier
Copy the EmailNotifier class, rename it SmsNotifier, and keep the email sending logic inside it
Add a type field to each notifier and an if-check inside the loop that handles SMS separately
Give SmsNotifier its own send(msg) method with the same parameters as the others

rubric: Matching the existing send(msg) interface lets polymorphism work with no loop changes.
Distractors change the loop, branch on type, or copy unrelated logic.

items.prompt: A class is defined as `class Counter: total = 0; def __init__(self): Counter.total += 1; self.id = Counter.total`. Objects a, b and c are created in that order. What is the value of `b.id + c.total`?
rubric: b.id was set to 2 when b was created, and the class-level total is 3 after three objects, so the sum is 5.
Choosing 4 or 6 comes from mixing up per-object and class-level state.

items.prompt: `Animal.speak()` returns "...". `Dog` overrides it to return "Woof". `Cat` does not override it. `Puppy` extends `Dog` and overrides `speak` to return `super().speak() + "!"`. What does `Puppy().speak() + Cat().speak()` produce?

options.label: Woof!...
Woof...
Woof!Woof

rubric: Puppy's super call reaches Dog's version, giving "Woof!", and Cat inherits Animal's "...".
Distractors ignore the inherited method or assume super reaches the wrong class.

items.prompt: You must ensure a bank account's balance can never go negative through withdrawals. Which implementation applies encapsulation correctly?

options.label: Keep balance protected so only subclasses change it, and trust each subclass to check the amount first
Keep balance private and add `withdraw(amount)` that rejects amounts above the balance before subtracting
Keep balance public and have each caller compare the amount with the balance before subtracting it
Keep balance private and add `setBalance(value)` that stores whatever value the caller passes in

rubric: Only a private field with a method that enforces the rule guarantees the invariant in one place.
A setter that stores anything, or caller-side checks, leave the rule unenforced.

items.prompt: `Employee(name, salary)` has a constructor that sets both fields. You write `Manager`, a subclass that adds a `bonus` field. Which constructor body for `Manager(name, salary, bonus)` is correct?

options.label: Assign only `this.bonus = bonus`, because name and salary are inherited and set automatically
Copy `name` and `salary` into new Manager-only fields, then assign `this.bonus = bonus`
Call `super(name, salary)` first, then assign `this.bonus = bonus`
Create a separate `Employee(name, salary)` object inside the constructor, then assign `bonus`

rubric: The parent constructor must run to initialise inherited state, so call super with the arguments.
Distractors assume automatic initialisation, duplicate fields, or build an unrelated parent object.

items.prompt: `OrderService` creates `new FileLogger()` inside its own constructor. You need to run it in tests with a fake logger that records messages. Which change achieves this?

options.label: Make every `FileLogger` method static so tests can call them without needing an instance of it
Add a boolean flag to `OrderService` that switches between real logging and fake logging at runtime
Subclass `OrderService` once per logger type and override the constructor in each subclass to choose it
Define a `Logger` interface and have `OrderService` receive a `Logger` through its constructor

rubric: Passing an interface-typed collaborator in lets tests supply a fake without changing the service.
Static methods, subclass-per-logger and flags keep the dependency hard-wired or clutter the class.

items.prompt: A `Cart` class has a public list field `items`, and other code adds invalid entries to it. Which changes apply encapsulation to fix this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Make `items` private and have `getItems()` return a read-only view or a copy
Keep `items` public but document that callers should not modify it directly
Make `items` private and add `setItems(list)` that stores the given list unchanged
Add `getItems()` that returns the internal list object itself so callers can read it
Make `items` private and add `addItem(item)` that validates the item before storing it

rubric: Validated mutation through a method and a read-only view or copy keep the list under the class's control.
Returning the internal list, public fields with documentation, or an unchecked setter still let invalid data in.

items.prompt: An `Invoice` export method uses `if format == 'pdf' ... else if format == 'csv' ...`. The team now has to add XML export and expects more formats later. They want to add XML without editing the existing PDF and CSV code. What should they do?

options.label: Define an `Exporter` interface with `export(invoice)`, one class per format, and pass in the exporter to use
Add another `else if` branch for XML in the existing method, so every format's logic stays together in one place and is easy to find
Copy the export method into a new `XmlInvoice` class and edit the copy to produce XML, leaving the original method untouched
Make `PdfExporter` a subclass of `CsvExporter` and XML a subclass of `PdfExporter`, so each new format reuses the earlier code

rubric: Polymorphism over a common interface lets a new format be added as a new class without touching existing code.
Extra branches, chained inheritance and copying all force edits to existing code or duplicate logic.

items.prompt: `Square` extends `Rectangle` and overrides `setWidth` so it also changes the height. Code written for `Rectangle` does `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4);` and expects `r.area()` to be 20, but gets 16 when `r` is a `Square`. What is the root cause?

options.label: The setters should be static so width and height are stored once per class, not per object
`Square` should have been created as an object inside `Rectangle` instead of being its own class
`Square` changes setter behaviour that `Rectangle` callers rely on, so it is not a safe substitute
`Rectangle.area()` multiplies width by height wrongly and must be overridden in every subclass

rubric: The subclass breaks the parent's behavioural contract, which is a substitutability violation.
Distractors blame static state, the area formula or object creation, none of which explains the 16.

items.prompt: `BaseList.addAll(items)` loops and calls `this.add(item)`. `CountingList` extends it, overrides both `add` and `addAll` to increase a counter, then calls super. After `addAll` with 3 items the counter reads 6. What explains this?

options.label: Overriding two methods makes most object-oriented languages run each override twice per call
The base class `add` is private, so the subclass version is called in its place on each element
The counter should be static, because a shared count would stop each list doubling its own total
`addAll` in the base class calls the overridden `add`, so each element is counted twice

rubric: The base class's internal call to an overridable method reaches the subclass override, so the counter increments twice per element.
Other options invent language behaviour or blame the counter's scope.

items.prompt: A unit test for `OrderService.placeOrder()` fails on a machine with no database, although the test only checks discount logic. Which design flaw best explains this?

options.label: `OrderService` exposes too many public methods, which forces each test to initialise a database first
Unit tests need to inherit from the repository class, and that inheritance hides the logic under test
The repository class is polymorphic, so every call made to it must reach the real database at runtime
`OrderService` builds a concrete database repository itself, so tests cannot avoid the real database

rubric: Hard-wired construction of a concrete collaborator couples the service to the database.
Public method count, test inheritance and polymorphism do not force a database dependency.

items.prompt: In Python, `class Bag: items = []` has `def add(self, x): self.items.append(x)`. After `b1 = Bag(); b2 = Bag(); b1.add(1)`, `b2.items` shows `[1]`. What is the cause?

options.label: `add` rebinds `self.items` to a fresh list on each call, and that rebinding leaks into other instances
In `add`, `self` refers to the class instead of the instance whenever the method is called on `b1`
Python copies class attributes lazily, so `b2` sees `b1`'s change until its first read of `items`
`items` belongs to the class, so both bags share one list that `append` mutates

rubric: A mutable class attribute is shared, and append mutates it in place without creating an instance attribute.
Other options misdescribe rebinding, self, or copying semantics.

items.prompt: Which situation is the strongest justification for using inheritance rather than composition?

options.label: `Car` needs an engine's start behaviour, so it extends `Engine` to avoid writing a few forwarding methods
`SavingsAccount` must be usable wherever an `Account` is expected, keeps all its behaviour, and adds interest
`Stack` wants a list's storage, so it extends `List` and hides most of the inherited methods from users
`Report` wants to reuse `Printer`'s print method, so it extends `Printer` even though a report is not a printer

rubric: A true is-a relationship with full substitutability and added behaviour fits inheritance.
The other cases reuse code without is-a, or hide inherited methods, which composition handles better.

items.prompt: Which observations show that class `Order` has poor encapsulation? Select all that apply.

options.label: `Order` implements a `Printable` interface that exposes a single `print()` method
Several other classes read `order.items` and `order.discount` to calculate totals themselves
Callers must call `setStatus('paid')` before `ship()` or the order ends in an invalid state
`Order` keeps its helper `roundMoney` private and uses it only inside its own methods

rubric: Outside code doing the object's work and callers needing a hidden call order both mean internal rules leak out of the class.
A private helper and a narrow interface are normal, healthy encapsulation.

items.prompt: In Java, `Payment`'s constructor calls `validate()` and `CardPayment` overrides `validate()` to check `merchantId.length() > 0`. `merchantId` is set in `CardPayment`'s constructor after `super(...)`. Creating a `CardPayment` throws a NullPointerException inside `validate()`. What is the root cause?

options.label: The base constructor calls overridable `validate()` before `merchantId` is set, so it sees null
The override runs on a half-built object only when `validate()` is declared public, so reducing its visibility would fix it
`CardPayment` replaces `validate()` instead of extending it, so the base class's fields are lost for the call
`merchantId` is a subclass field, so the inherited `validate()` call cannot be bound to it before the constructor ends

rubric: The base constructor runs first and dispatches to the override while the subclass fields are still uninitialised.
Other options invent rules about overriding, field access or call order.

items.prompt: A `CountingList` extends `ArrayList` and overrides `add(x)` and `addAll(c)`, each incrementing a counter and then calling `super`. After `addAll` with 3 items, the counter reads 6. The base `addAll` internally calls `add` per element. What is the root cause?

options.label: The counter is an instance field, so each call to a different overridden method keeps its own separate count
Calling `super` in an override re-runs the parent method for collection arguments, so each element is added twice
The override of `addAll` should be marked `final`, since the base class then skips its per-element calls to `add`
The base `addAll` calls the overridable `add`, so the subclass's override also runs per element

rubric: Inheritance breaks encapsulation: the subclass depends on how the base class calls its own methods (fragile base class).
Distractors blame static state or super semantics, which are unrelated to the double dispatch.

items.prompt: `Square` extends `Rectangle`, and `Square.setWidth` also sets the height. A client does `r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4);` on a `Rectangle` reference and asserts `r.area() == 20`. With a `Square` it gets 16. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: `Square` strengthens an invariant the base type's contract does not allow, so it is not substitutable for `Rectangle`
The bug arises because setters were used; direct public field access would have avoided the substitution problem
`Square` lacks an `area` override, so it falls back to a wrong computation inherited from `Rectangle`
The assertion is wrong, because area should always be recomputed from the last assigned side only

rubric: This is a Liskov substitution violation: the subclass adds a constraint that breaks the base contract of independent sides.
Distractors treat it as a missing override or a setter-style issue rather than a contract violation.

items.prompt: An `Order` class keeps its `items` list `private` but has `getItems()` returning the internal `ArrayList`. Another module calls `order.getItems().clear()`, and the order total becomes inconsistent with its stored `total` field. What is the underlying flaw?

options.label: The `total` field is cached in the object, so it should be recomputed in the constructor and never stored again
The getter returns a live reference to mutable internal state, so `private` no longer protects the invariant
The `items` field should be `protected` so that only subclasses of `Order` can modify the list contents directly
The getter is named like an accessor, so callers assume it is read-only and skip the checks a setter would have

rubric: Encapsulation protects invariants, not just field visibility; leaking a mutable reference lets callers bypass them.
Distractors focus on access modifiers or naming, which miss the aliasing problem.

items.prompt: A base class constructor calls an overridable `init()` method. A subclass overrides `init()` to use its own field `name = "x"`, assigned in a field initializer. At runtime `init()` sees `name` as null. Why?

options.label: Field initializers run only when the object is accessed through a reference of the subclass's exact type
The subclass field initializers run only after the base constructor finishes, so `init()` executes before `name` is set
The field `name` is garbage collected after the base constructor completes, which leaves it null in the subclass
The override of `init()` is ignored during construction, so the base version runs and cannot see `name`

rubric: Construction order runs the base constructor first, yet virtual dispatch already selects the subclass override.
Distractor 2 is the common belief that overrides are not dispatched in constructors.

items.prompt: A `Point` class overrides `equals` to compare x and y, but not `hashCode`. Two equal points are added to a `HashSet`, and the set reports size 2. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: Equal points get different default hash codes, so they usually land in different buckets and `equals` is never called
The `equals` override must have the wrong parameter type, so the set cannot identify duplicates for any class that defines it
`HashSet` rejects objects whose class defines `equals` without `compareTo`, so it stores both of them separately
`HashSet` compares elements by reference first, so `equals` is never consulted for any objects stored in the set

rubric: Hash-based collections use the hash code to choose a bucket, so equal objects need equal hashes.
Distractors misdescribe how the collection uses equals.

items.prompt: A team has `Stack extends ArrayList`, `Manager extends Employee`, `Logger extends Database` (to reuse its connection), and `Circle extends Shape`. Which cases show inheritance used where an is-a relationship does not hold or the base contract is exposed wrongly? Select all that apply.

options.label: `Manager extends Employee`, since a manager is an employee with extra responsibilities
`Stack extends ArrayList`, since it exposes index-based insertion that breaks stack discipline
`Circle extends Shape`, since a circle is a kind of shape with area and perimeter
`Logger extends Database`, since it is reuse of code without a real is-a relationship

rubric: Stack exposes unwanted inherited operations and Logger reuses code with no is-a relationship; composition fits both.
Circle and Manager are genuine specialisations.

items.prompt: A `Notification` class has a `type` string field. Methods `send()`, `format()` and `priority()` each contain an if/else chain on `type` ("email", "sms", "push"). Adding "slack" took edits in all three methods, and one was missed, causing a production bug. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The chains should use `switch` instead, because the bug came from if/else syntax being error-prone and a switch makes missing cases easier to spot
The methods are too long, so splitting each into smaller helper methods would remove the need to edit all three when a type is added
Type-specific behaviour is scattered across methods, so each new variant forces edits everywhere; polymorphism would localise it
The class should make `type` private, because exposing it let callers set an unexpected value that the other methods did not handle

rubric: Repeated type switches signal missing polymorphism; variant knowledge should live in one place per type.
Other options treat syntax, visibility or length rather than the structural duplication.

items.prompt: A game has enemies that can fly, swim, shoot and explode, in many combinations that designers change often. Criteria: avoid class explosion, allow behaviour changes without editing existing classes, keep the design simple. Which approach is best?

options.label: One `Enemy` class with boolean flags and conditionals in each method to pick the behaviour
A subclass for every combination, such as `FlyingShootingEnemy`, with each type fully explicit
Multiple inheritance of every capability into one `Enemy` class, with unused ones switched off at runtime
An `Enemy` composed of swappable movement and attack strategy objects, configured per enemy

rubric: Composition with strategies handles combinations without subclass explosion and permits runtime changes.
Hierarchies explode and flags centralise conditionals, which breaks open-closed.

items.prompt: `Invoice`, `Image` and `Sensor` classes are unrelated, but each must be `Exportable` to JSON. They share no state, and each already extends a different framework base class. Criteria: no forced shared state, works with single inheritance, minimal coupling. Best choice?

options.label: An `Exportable` interface that each class implements with its own export logic
A utility class with a static `export(Object)` method using type checks for each class
A common `Entity` base class placed above the framework classes so all three inherit from it
An abstract class `Exportable` with a protected buffer that all three classes extend

rubric: An interface expresses the capability without state and fits single-inheritance constraints.
An abstract class cannot be used because they already extend other bases; static type checks do not extend well.

items.prompt: A `Money` value (amount, currency) is used as a key in hash maps, shared among threads, and passed into many modules. Criteria: safe sharing, stable hashing, minimal defensive copying. Which design is best?

options.label: Mutable with setters, and every caller makes a defensive copy before storing it
Immutable, with operations returning new instances and `equals`/`hashCode` based on both fields
Mutable with setters guarded by a `synchronized` keyword so all threads see consistent values
Mutable but frozen after first use through a flag that makes later setters throw exceptions

rubric: Immutability gives thread safety and stable hash keys without copying.
Synchronised setters still allow a key to change while stored in a map.

items.prompt: A compiler has a fixed set of 6 AST node types that will not change, but new operations (type-check, optimise, pretty-print, emit) are added every sprint. Criteria: cheap addition of operations, few files touched per new operation. Which is best?

options.label: Generate a subclass per operation and node pair, so each combination gets its own dedicated class
Put each operation as a virtual method in every node class so nodes own all of their behaviour
Use a visitor or pattern-matching function per operation, so a new operation touches one place
Keep a type string on nodes and let each operation parse it with ad hoc conditionals everywhere

rubric: With a stable type set and growing operations, visitor or pattern matching localises each new operation.
Virtual methods suit the opposite case, with new types frequently added.

items.prompt: `ReportService` creates its own `SmtpMailer` with `new SmtpMailer()` inside its methods. Criteria: unit tests must run without network, mail provider may change, minimal added complexity. Which change is best?

options.label: Make `SmtpMailer` a singleton and have tests set a flag that suppresses all network sending
Add a `MailSender` interface and pass an implementation into `ReportService`'s constructor
Wrap the `new SmtpMailer()` call in try/catch and ignore connection failures during tests
Subclass `ReportService` in tests and override every method that touches the mailer

rubric: Constructor injection of an abstraction allows fakes in tests and provider swaps with little complexity.
The others keep hidden coupling or mix test logic into production code.

items.prompt: Judge which conditions favour an object-oriented design over a plain procedural script with data structures. Criteria: long-lived code, multiple contributors. Select all that apply.

options.label: The program is a one-off 40-line data conversion with a single input and output
Several entity types share an interface but vary in behaviour, and new variants are expected
The only goal is to use classes in every module regardless of how data and behaviour relate
Invariants must be enforced consistently around data that many parts of the code touch

rubric: Varying behaviour behind an interface and invariant protection are where objects pay off.
A tiny one-off script gains little, and using classes everywhere is not a design criterion.

items.prompt: A team models payment methods with `Payment` -> `CardPayment` -> `CreditCardPayment` -> `RewardsCreditCardPayment`, and now must add per-country fee rules and fraud checks that vary independently of the method. Criteria: independent variation, shallow hierarchy, easy testing. What is the best direction?

options.label: Move fee and fraud code into the deepest subclass and have its ancestors call it through casts
Keep the hierarchy shallow and inject fee-rule and fraud-check strategies into `Payment`
Add country and fraud flags to `Payment` and branch on them inside each method
Add subclasses per country, for example `GermanRewardsCreditCardPayment`, to hold the fee rules

rubric: Independent axes of variation call for composition with injected strategies, which keeps the hierarchy shallow and easy to test.
Country subclasses multiply classes; flags and casts entangle concerns.

items.prompt: A team makes `Square` extend `Rectangle`, where `Rectangle` has independent `setWidth` and `setHeight` and `Square` overrides both to set both sides. Judge this design on whether a `Square` can safely stand in for a `Rectangle` in existing callers.

options.label: Sound: overriding both setters keeps the area formula correct, and area is the main contract callers rely on
Sound: a square is a rectangle in mathematics, so callers written against Rectangle stay safe with a Square
Flawed: overriding inherited setters breaks the base contract, so a subclass can't change them and stay substitutable
Flawed: callers expect width and height to change independently, and Square breaks that, so it can't substitute

rubric: Substitutability depends on behavioural contracts such as independent dimensions, not on real-world 'is-a' relations.
Distractors rely on the mathematical is-a intuition or on an overly absolute rule about overriding.

items.prompt: Three unrelated classes (`Invoice`, `Shipment`, `User`) all need audit logging. Criteria: the logging policy must be swappable at runtime, and none of the classes may be coupled to a shared base class's internals. Which approach is best?

options.label: Copy the logging code into each class as private methods, which removes all shared coupling between the three
Use a static `Logger` utility with a global switch flag, so every class changes policy together at runtime
Give each class an injected `AuditPolicy` collaborator and delegate to it, so the policy swaps without any hierarchy
Make each extend an `AuditedEntity` base class that holds the logging code and exposes protected hooks to tweak it

rubric: Composition with an injected policy meets both criteria: runtime swapping and no base-class coupling.
The base class option couples subclasses to its internals, and the static switch cannot vary the policy per object.

items.prompt: A reviewer says: 'This class is well encapsulated because every field is private and has a public getter and setter.' Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: Correct: setters are the natural place to validate input, so adding them for every field always strengthens a class
Incorrect: encapsulation requires fields to be protected rather than private, so subclasses can reach the shared state
Incorrect: accessors for every field expose the representation and let callers break invariants, so little is hidden
Correct: private fields with accessors hide the data, and that is all encapsulation requires of a class design

rubric: Encapsulation protects invariants and hides design decisions; blanket accessors leak the representation.
Distractors equate encapsulation with field visibility or treat setters as inherently protective.

items.prompt: A subclass of a collection overrides `add` and `addAll` to count insertions, but the base `addAll` internally calls `add`, so counts double. Criterion: the fix must survive future changes to the base class's internals. Which fix is best?

options.label: Make the counter `static` and reset it inside `addAll`, so repeated calls from the base are never tallied twice
Override `addAll` to add the count, call `super.addAll`, then subtract the duplicates the base class creates per element
Wrap the collection in a forwarding class that counts in its own `add` and `addAll`, delegating to the inner one
Stop overriding `addAll` and rely on the base `add` calls, since the base class currently calls it internally

rubric: Forwarding composition doesn't depend on whether the base addAll calls add, so it is robust to change.
The other options encode today's implementation details of the base class and break if they change.

items.prompt: A compiler has a stable set of 6 AST node types, but new analyses (optimiser, printer, type checker) are added every month. Judged on the cost of adding an operation, which structure is best?

options.label: A `type` string on each node plus copied node logic, so analyses can read the string and branch when needed
A deeper node hierarchy with an abstract class per analysis, so nodes inherit each analysis from a new parent
A visitor, or pattern matching over a closed set of nodes, so each analysis sits in one place without editing nodes
A virtual method per operation on each node class, so every new analysis is one more method in all six nodes

rubric: With stable types and growing operations, grouping operations outside the nodes minimises edits per new operation.
Virtual methods favour adding types, not operations; the other options add duplication or hierarchy without solving it.

items.prompt: Which situations are good evidence that a class-based object model is a poor fit for a part of a system? Select all that apply.

options.label: Work is a pipeline of stateless transformations over plain records, with no identity or lifecycle to protect
Many interchangeable payment providers must be swapped behind one stable interface at runtime
Third parties must extend behaviour by supplying new implementations without editing the core code
The set of data shapes is fixed, while new operations over them are added constantly across teams
Entities hold state with invariants that must hold across many operations during their lifetimes

rubric: Stateless data pipelines and fixed shapes with growing operations favour functional or data-oriented styles.
The other options describe polymorphism, invariants and extension points, where objects fit well.

items.prompt: A base class `Widget` constructor calls an overridable `init()`. The subclass `ChartWidget` overrides `init()` using a field assigned in its own constructor, so startup throws a null error. There are 30 subclasses. Judged on robustness across all of them, which remedy is best?

options.label: Remove the constructor call and let a factory build each widget, then call `init()` once the object is complete
Mark `init()` as `final` in the base class and move all the subclass logic into the base constructor body
Reorder each subclass constructor to assign its fields before calling `super(...)`, wherever the language allows
Add null checks inside each subclass `init()` so startup tolerates the unset field until the constructors finish

rubric: Calling overridable methods from constructors exposes half-built objects; a factory runs init after construction.
Null checks patch symptoms 30 times, and the reordering option is often illegal or fragile.

items.prompt: Design a payment module. Constraints: third parties ship new payment methods as separate modules, the core must not be recompiled or depend on any concrete method, and each method validates its own configuration. Which design meets all constraints?

options.label: The core defines a `PaymentMethod` interface with `validate()`; modules implement it and register with a core registry
The core defines an abstract `PaymentMethod` class and ships every subclass itself, each validating its own settings
The core holds an enum of methods and a switch calling each validator, updated whenever a new module is released
The core imports each module's concrete class and calls its `validate()`, using a config file to list active ones

rubric: An interface plus registry inverts the dependency so modules plug in without core changes.
The enum, bundled subclasses and concrete imports all force core edits or recompilation for new methods.

items.prompt: Design `Money` for a billing library. Constraints: an amount never changes after creation, negative amounts are invalid, and adding different currencies must never happen silently. Which design meets all three?

options.label: An immutable class with a public constructor, where `add` returns the left amount when the currencies differ
Public mutable `amount` and `currency` fields, with a `validate()` method that callers invoke before each use
A class with private fields and setters rejecting negatives, where `add` silently converts the other side to match
An immutable class built through a validating factory, where `add` returns a new `Money` or throws on mismatch

rubric: Immutability, factory validation and a failing add on mismatch cover all three constraints.
Distractors allow mutation, skip validation at construction, or hide currency mismatches silently.

items.prompt: A proposed event design has a `Subject` holding a list of `Listener` objects with `subscribe(listener)` and `notify()`. Short-lived UI panels subscribe when created. The design must avoid memory leaks and stale callbacks. What is it missing?

options.label: A way for listeners to unsubscribe, or for the subject to hold them weakly, so discarded panels can be released
A `synchronized` keyword on `notify()` and `subscribe()`, so panels created on different threads never modify or traverse the list at once
A second list of listeners sorted by priority, so the important panels are told before the less important ones are
A common abstract base class for all listeners, so the subject can call each one through a single parent type

rubric: Strong references with no deregistration keep dead panels alive and still receiving callbacks.
The other options address typing, threading or ordering, not object lifetime.

items.prompt: Design `Order` so that no code can push the total of its lines above a credit limit, even though many modules read the lines. Which design meets this?

options.label: `Order` exposes a mutable `lines` list, and a nightly `checkLimit()` job flags any order that went over the limit
`Order` is the only way to change lines, via methods that enforce the limit, and it exposes only read-only views
`Order` copies the limit into every `OrderLine`, so each line validates itself whenever any module edits it
`Order` returns its internal list, and each `OrderLine` setter checks the limit against its parent order

rubric: An aggregate root that controls all mutation and exposes read-only views can enforce the invariant.
The other options let outside code mutate the list or check too late or too locally.

items.prompt: A `Bird` base class has `fly()`, and `Penguin` throws on it. Redesign so callers needing flight can never receive a penguin, with no runtime type checks and no exceptions for unsupported operations. Which design works?

options.label: Keep `fly()` on `Bird` and add `canFly()`, which callers must check before each call to avoid the exception
Have `Penguin` override `fly()` to do nothing, so calls are harmless and no exception reaches any caller
Split into `Bird` and a `Flyer` interface that flying birds implement, with flight-needing callers accepting `Flyer`
Add a `FlightlessBird` subclass of `Bird` and use `instanceof` in callers to skip it before calling `fly()`

rubric: Segregating a capability interface lets the type system exclude penguins from flight-needing callers.
The other options keep an unsupported operation on the base type or rely on runtime checks.

items.prompt: A `ReportGenerator` base class must fix the order: validate, gather, format, publish. Subclasses customise gather, format and publish but must never skip or reorder validation. Which design elements together meet this? Select all that apply.

options.label: A `final` (non-overridable) `run()` method in the base class that calls the steps in order
Abstract protected `gather`, `format` and `publish` steps that subclasses must implement
A public `validate()` documented as 'call this first' for subclass authors
A private or final `validate()` step that `run()` always calls first
A public, overridable `run()` so subclasses can adapt the order to their needs

rubric: A final template method, overridable steps and a locked validation step enforce the order and the customisation points.
Overridable run() or documentation-only conventions cannot guarantee validation happens first.

items.prompt: A reporting tool has 12 subclasses such as `PdfEmailReport` and `CsvS3Report`, one per format-and-destination pair. Product wants to add formats and destinations independently, without writing a subclass for every combination. Which redesign meets that?

options.label: Create mixin classes per format and destination, then write a subclass combining one of each for every pair
Give `Report` a `format` and a `destination` string and one large `switch` that handles every combination inside
Add one `Report` subclass level for formats and another below it for destinations, creating a deeper hierarchy
`Report` holds a `Formatter` and a `Destination` collaborator, each with its own implementations, chosen at construction

rubric: Composing two independent strategies avoids the combinatorial subclass explosion (bridge-like design).
Deeper hierarchies, switches and per-pair mixin subclasses still need work for every combination.
